title: 3 English Teachers Guide Grade 1
text:
This English Teacher’s Guide uses research based pedagogy to support pupils to develop into
 successful English language readers. These materials were piloted by the Ministry of Education,
 Science & Technology and USAID during the three year Primary Reading and Maths Initiative (PRIMR)
 programme. It focuses on the essential skills for literacy, including recognizing letters and their sounds,
 putting letter sounds together to read words, putting words together accurately to make meaning
 from text, and to write interesting stories. The content and skills taught in this English Teacher’s Guide
 cover the Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) syllabus covering the four areas of
 literacy: listening, speaking, reading, and writing, as well as the curricular themes. Among the many
 attributes of this English Teacher’s Guide are:
 • Exciting practical activities to teach all the themes in the KICD syllabus.
 • Activities that are displayed in a logical order based on research in teaching and learning English
 • Colourful illustrations closely related to the stories and pupil’s lives, making learning very interesting
 • Interesting, culturally relevant and age appropriate stories for practising and improving all skills
 related to reading
 • Controlled text stories written at pupils’ reading level allowing for independent reading and
 comprehension even in the first weeks of school
 • Teacher read aloud stories to develop oral vocabulary and listening comprehension skills
 This guide was developed by an experienced technical team from the Ministry of Education Science
 and Technology (MOEST), the Teacher Service Commission (TSC), the Kenya Education Management
 Institute (KEMI), the Kenya Institute of Special Education (KISE) and USAID’s Tusome Early Grade
 Reading Activity.
 This book was produced with support
 from the U.S. Agency for International
 Development (USAID) and Department for
 International Development (DFID) through
 the USAID Tusome Early Grade Reading
 Activity.

 Foreword
 Since independence the Government of Kenya has recognized education as a basic human right and is
 therefore committed to the provision of education to all her citizens. Significant resources have been
 invested towards improving access, relevance, equity and quality resulting in significant improvement
 in infrastructure and increased enrolment in all sub sectors of education and training.
 The government realizes that to be internationally competitive and economically viable, the country
 requires an education system that will produce citizens who are innovative and are able to engage in
 lifelong learning and perform complex tasks. The education system should also produce individuals
 capable of problem-solving, taking decisions, require minimal supervision, assume responsibility, and
 have better reading, quantitative reasoning and expository skills.
 Sustainable development demands that every human being acquires the 21st century knowledge,
 skills, attitudes and values necessary to shape a sustainable future. Emphasis is on education for
 developing competencies in literacy and numeracy. Kenya has made progress in improving the quality
 of education. This is reflected in the number of programmes designed to address quality issues,
 particularly in the area of literacy in lower primary.
 This Tusome book will no doubt inform and guide teaching and learning in lower primary in the area
 of literacy. The design of the book ensures that all Kenyan children can read and comprehend by
 the end of the year. I thereby urge our partners to continue supporting the education sector in the
 implementation of strategies to promote the quality of education.
 Cabinet Secretary
 Preface
 The goal of the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology is to provide quality education to
 all learners irrespective of their socio-economic status. Reforms have been undertaken to improve
 the education sector with a view to making it globally competitive. Research initiatives such as
 National Assessment Monitoring Learning Achievement (NASMLA) and Southern and Eastern Africa
 Consortium for Monitoring Education Quality (SACMEQ) indicate the need for improved achievement
 in literacy and numeracy competencies.
 Recent developments in Kenya have made the need for a comprehensive quality framework even more
 urgent. These changes are embodied in the Constitution of Kenya 2010 and Kenya Vision 2030. The
 Kenya Constitution provides for Free and Compulsory Basic Education to all children, while Vision
 2030 has an ultimate goal to transform the country into a globally competitive and prosperous nation
 by 2030. Among its aspirations is the provision of high quality education and training to produce a
 highly skilled labor force and an education system that is linked to the global market and industry.
 The Sessional Paper No. 14 of 2012 provides for appropriate pathways and 100% transition in Basic
 Education levels without compromising the quality of education.
 The Ministry has had an increasing focus on the quality of education in lower primary, particularly
 in the areas of literacy and numeracy. The Tusome national literacy programme will improve literacy
 outcomes in Classes 1 and 2. The programme, which is supported by USAID and DFID, aims to
 improve teacher capacity for effective delivery methods of classroom instruction, improve access
 to appropriate textbooks and supplementary materials in literacy, enhance instructional support
 supervision of teachers by Teacher Advisory Center ( TAC) Tutors and head teachers, establish
 an effective and eficient monitoring and evaluation system, which links instructional practice and
 learning outcomes in literacy. It will also enhance the use of ICT to support literacy outcomes and
 enhance the capacity of the education sector to sustainably improve literacy outcomes.
 On behalf of the Ministry, I urge all stakeholders to join hands in ensuring the implementation of the
 Tusome programme is successful.
 Principal Secretary, State Department of Education

 Guide to the teacher
 This Teacher’s Guide helps teachers instruct learners in the fundamental skills in reading
 that are necessary for improving fluency in reading and comprehension. The teacher,
 in this approach, utilizes more balanced strategies to teaching and presents a diverse
 set of activities within classrooms. While the approach gives room for the teacher’s
 creativity, teacher’s preparation still remains key to the success of the lesson in this
 guide. Teachers are encouraged to devise and use relevant and contextually applicable
 teaching and learning resources that will enhance mastery of the content taught. Such
 resources may include, but are not limited to, a dictionary, pictures, murals and realias.
 While blackboard usage is important and encouraged in this guide, the approach lays
 emphasis on learners having their own individual textbooks, where they track letters and
 words to increase their exposure to text. In addition, there are exercises in the Pupil’s
 Books that learners need to practice independently. These exercises can be used during
 classwork or as extended homework. Homework assignments are provided. Teachers need
 to encourage learners to do these activities at home. This is aimed at ensuring guardian
 or parental participation. Teachers are encouraged to find time to check learners’ work
 to ensure the activities are done and formative feedback is given in a timely manner.
 Teachers are encouraged to choose the most appropriate activity that will make the
 learners understand the concept taught. Such activities include the use of pictures,
 demonstrations, role playing or explanations using words that are familiar, simple and
 short.
 This Teacher’s Guide has been designed in a way that removes barriers to learning for all
 learners regardless of their abilities or impairments. Learners with learning impairments
 include those with mild to moderately severe challenges. Such learners may be (and have
 always been) supported by their teachers in several ways. The following are various ways
 that a teacher can support learners with various learning impairments:
 Hearing impaired: Let the learner sit near the teacher. The teacher should identify and
 use relevant realia or pictorials as teaching and learning materials.
 Visually impaired: Let the learner sit either near or far from the board depending on
 where they can see well. Avoid visual disruptors such as reflective mirrors in classroom.
 Identify and use relevant realia or pictorials as teaching and learning materials.
 Learning difficulties: Set aside more time for remedial teaching. Teach at a slower pace
 and encourage the learners no matter how small effort they make.
 Speech disorders: Be patient with the child and give them more time to complete their
 sentences. Formatively encourage the learner in their efforts however small.
 Gifted and talented: Give the pupil additional or more challenging tasks to stimulate
 their brain. Give the learner opportunities to grow their talents.
 If any of the suggested ways do not work, teachers are encouraged to refer the child for
 further professional help.

 Introduction
 This teachers’ guide was created with the guidance of international and local
 reading and language experts in a carefully designed process. During an initial
 workshop with MOEST and KICD staff, a Scope and Sequence was designed that
 became the road map for lesson plan development. In the workshop, decisions
 were made about the order in which the letters will be taught in both languages,
 what specific activities would be used as part of the instructional methodology,
 and when to begin teaching English reading skills.
 In Kiswahili, the scope and sequence is based on the frequency of letter sounds,
 teaching the most common letter sounds first so that learners could learn to read
 words and sentences by the end of the first two weeks of instruction. Stories were
 carefully crafted so that the majority of words contained only sounds learners have
 already been taught. The English scope and sequence focuses on the development
 of oral language in the first six weeks, based on the themes of the KICD syllabus
 and the vocabulary needed to understand words and stories, which are read in
 later weeks. These first six weeks’ of instruction include vocabulary building and
 listening comprehension activities. No English reading skills will be taught until
 learners have learned the basic vocabulary necessary to make meaning. From
 week seven, the lessons follow a scope and sequence of teaching letter sounds and
 words similar to that of Kiswahili, but carefully designed to produce English stories
 that relate thematically to the KICD syllabus and give pupils ample practice with
 new sounds and words. The idea is that learners will be introduced to English
 letters from week seven onwards that they have already learned in Kiswahili. The
 letter sound lessons in English explicitly tell learners which sounds are the same
 in Kiswahili and English and which sounds are different, allowing for more efficient
 use of learner and teacher time.
 Each lesson plan consists of several activities designed to teach learners the specific
 skills needed to be successful readers. The activities cover the four components of
 literacy (listening, speaking, reading and writing), as well as the five components
 of reading (phonemic awareness, alphabetic principle, fluency, vocabulary and
 comprehension). These components cover the range of skills critical to early
 literacy. Lesson plans focus on the key ideas, that each letter represents a sound
 and these letters are put together to form words. Words have meaning. Words
 are put together to form simple sentences. Sentences make up a story. Each day
 learners learn and practise letters, words, story reading and comprehension. The
 fifth day of each week consists of review and assessment activities so that teachers
 can follow individual learner progress.

 This English Teacher’s Guide uses research based pedagogy to support pupils to develop into
 successful English language readers. These materials were piloted by the Ministry of Education,
 Science & Technology and USAID during the three year Primary Reading and Maths Initiative (PRIMR)
 programme. It focuses on the essential skills for literacy, including recognizing letters and their sounds,
 putting letter sounds together to read words, putting words together accurately to make meaning
 from text, and to write interesting stories. The content and skills taught in this English Teacher’s Guide
 cover the Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) syllabus covering the four areas of
 literacy: listening, speaking, reading, and writing, as well as the curricular themes. Among the many
 attributes of this English Teacher’s Guide are:
 • Exciting practical activities to teach all the themes in the KICD syllabus.
 • Activities that are displayed in a logical order based on research in teaching and learning English
 • Colourful illustrations closely related to the stories and pupil’s lives, making learning very interesting
 • Interesting, culturally relevant and age appropriate stories for practising and improving all skills
 related to reading
 • Controlled text stories written at pupils’ reading level allowing for independent reading and
 comprehension even in the first weeks of school
 • Teacher read aloud stories to develop oral vocabulary and listening comprehension skills
 This guide was developed by an experienced technical team from the Ministry of Education Science
 and Technology (MOEST), the Teacher Service Commission (TSC), the Kenya Education Management
 Institute (KEMI), the Kenya Institute of Special Education (KISE) and USAID’s Tusome Early Grade
 Reading Activity.
 This book was produced with support
 from the U.S. Agency for International
 Development (USAID) and Department for
 International Development (DFID) through
 the USAID Tusome Early Grade Reading
 Activity.
